title: Remembering the rose-apple tree
hookLine: he recalls the boyhood joy under the tree: could that be the way (MN 36)
last: SIX YEARS — HARDER ISN'T ALWAYS BETTER.

lines: THE END OF THE HARD WAY.
cards: Sometimes, when you've been stuck on a problem for hours, the answer arrives in the shower. Or on a walk. Or right as you're falling asleep.
Not from pushing harder. From somewhere you'd stopped looking. The wanderer has reached the end of the hard way.
The breath, the fasting, the pain: he has pushed each one as far as it goes, and none of it has worked. So he sits, thin as a shadow, and asks: could there be another way to awakening?
And a memory comes back, the one from day twenty-seven. This time, not the memory itself, but what it did to him.

teach.b: On day twenty-seven, the boy sat in the shade. Today it's the man, and the same memory lands very differently. In the Buddha's account, it comes in three steps.
First, the memory: once, while his father the Sakyan was working, he sat in the cool shade of a rose-apple tree, and his mind settled into the first jhana, a calm, secluded joy.
Second, a question: could that be the path to awakening?
Third, the answer, which came right after the memory: that is the path. Look where he's sitting when this happens.
Not in a palace, not as a beginner, but at the far end of years of hardship, with everything he's built his search on in pieces. He has been treating ease as the enemy.

teach.h: WHY AM I AFRAID OF THAT JOY?
teach.b: Now he asks himself, why am I afraid of that happiness, a happiness that has nothing to do with sensual pleasure or anything unwholesome? I'm not afraid of it, he answers. That's a reversal.
The clue had been in his own past the whole time, while he looked for the answer in pain. Then comes the hard, practical part.

teach.h: NOT IN THIS BODY. I WILL EAT.
teach.b: He looks at his body, all bones, and says plainly: it isn't easy to reach that kind of joy with a body this worn out.
So, he decides, I will eat some solid food. The memory doesn't just comfort him. It changes his plan.

how: Buddhist meditation traditions teach cultivating calm joy (piti and sukha) as part of concentration, and MN 36 is read as the turn from austerity toward the way he would later teach.

games.q: you know now where the path is: a calm joy you once knew. but your body is all bones. what do you do?
o: fast harder, to prove you're serious.
eat some solid food, to have the strength.
go back to the palace to rest.
games.why: he decides to eat solid food. the memory didn't just comfort him; it changed his plan.

practice: Remember a small moment of easy calm from this past week, a quiet minute with a cup of something hot, sunlight across a floor, a walk where nothing needed doing, and let it come back with its temperature, sounds and smell.
Then ask it, the way he asked his: what was absent, what was present, that let the calm come? Don't force an answer; just notice what the body does with the remembering.

wordCard.voice: Jambu. The rose-apple tree under which the wanderer recalled a calm joy from boyhood, and realized it pointed the way.

orig.note: Pali: jambu, the tree usually translated rose-apple, whose shade sheltered the boy.

carryVoice: Your line: the joy was a clue. Following a clue means doing something different. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahasaccaka Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 36): the memory of the first jhana
